extracted.intended_audience: academics, grant applicants, and researchers interested in peer review and research evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the criteria and informal standards panelists use to assess academic grant proposals, including formal criteria (significance, originality, methods, clarity) and informal criteria (intelligence, elegance, cultural capital, moral qualities). Useful for understanding how reviewers judge proposals across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance stands out as one of the most important formal criteria used by panelists when evaluating proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance can be measured in different registers — social importance, intellectual or theoretical importance. The chapter notes that 'significance . . . stand out as the most important of the formal criteria used' and that what counts as significant varies across disciplines and may be understood in social or theoretical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality (or originality/novelty) is a top formal criterion used to assess proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality is valued as breaking new ground; panelists praise risk-takers and projects that challenge received views. The chapter stresses that 'originality' is defined in many ways across fields and that valuing originality can advantage those who signal 'cutting-edge' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of expression and argument is a formal criterion mentioned by panelists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity includes well-written proposals and the ability to express complex ideas in an orderly fashion. Good writing is tied to 'elegance' and 'getting the language right.' Lack of clarity or excessive jargon can make work seem 'boring' or hard to evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods / Methodological rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of methods and methodological rigor is a standard formal criterion (listed after significance and originality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods are valued but defined differently across aims: methodological rigor means different things for projects aiming at theoretical generalization versus case-based demonstrations. In noninterpretative disciplines, panelists emphasize understanding what is being tested and the chance of significant results; methodological tools (surveys, stats, qualitative software) play a central role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists look for 'signs of intelligence' in applicants and proposals (three-quarters mention at least one dimension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from respondents include 'subtlety and complexity with which the project is framed' and 'ability to understand and present complex ideas in an orderly fashion, to balance potentially conflicting positions.' Intellectual virtuosity—making sense of complex phenomena—is prized. In elite settings, intelligence is seen as a nuanced mix of traits (nimbleness, listening, subtlety).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Being articulate is treated as a positive sign of intellectual quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulateness signals ability to communicate ideas clearly in panels and proposals; in elite interviews it is valued when it 'establishes a circuit of exchange' rather than dominating others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent
rubrics_metrics.description: Competence—demonstrated command of one’s area and methodological skill—is a criterion reviewers mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence can temper subjective reactions to 'interesting' work: some panelists subordinate intrinsic interest to competence, ensuring the project is really asking and able to answer substantive questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligent
rubrics_metrics.description: General intelligence (as perceived by reviewers) functions as an evaluative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers infer intelligence from framing, subtlety, complexity, and the candidate's ability to think nimble and clearly. Intelligence is intertwined with ability to synthesize literature and capture essential elements of problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talented
rubrics_metrics.description: Talent (an assessed capacity beyond competence) is cited as part of the informal criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talent is often described in exemplars (intellectual heroes) and is associated with creativity, flair, and the ability to produce exceptional synthetic insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance (writing and argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance—'a kind of perfectionism, trying to get the language right'—is an aesthetic criterion valued especially in the humanities and history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance includes clear, not overly rococo prose, a strong personal voice, and felicitous interpretative writing (e.g., Geertz's cockfight essay). It often overlaps with display of cultural capital; valuing elegance risks conflating excellence with elite stylistic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural capital / display of cultural ease
rubrics_metrics.description: Display of cultural capital (cultural ease and breadth) is used as an informal evaluative signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists note familiarity with high-status cultural signals (literacy, breadth) as indicative of scholarly fit. The text warns this can disadvantage applicants from working-class backgrounds and may conflate excellence with elite membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting / Exciting
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived intrinsic interest or excitement about a project is an important informal criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Murray Davis is quoted: 'interesting theories deny certain assumptions of their audience.' Panelists want writers to convey passion and importance: 'if it’s not important enough to excite them, then why should they get funding?' However, evaluators differ on weighting interest versus competence; some subordinate interest to methodological soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boring (negative criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boringness is a negative evaluative label tied to repetition, reliance on the same analysis, or heavy jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work seen as repetitive or filled with jargon may be dismissed. One historian criticized certain fields as 'extremely... boring' and 'artificially constructed'—a reason for devaluing proposals despite technical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination / work ethic
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination and strong work ethic are moral qualities valued in applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers praise trajectories showing will and overcoming hardship; examples include a student whose 'trajectory and sheer will' revealed strengths that led to success. Determination signals the likelihood of project completion and sustained productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility / modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility or unpretentiousness is viewed positively, especially when paired with expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A modest presentation—'without being overbearing or patronizing'—is admired. Overly self-promoting or arrogant tones can unsettle reviewers, though brilliance may sometimes override distaste for arrogance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity (being true to one’s own intellectual commitments rather than following trends) is a prized moral/intellectual quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity manifests as pursuing less popular paths passionately; reviewers value applicants who are 'passionately attached' to a subject and demonstrate 'a distinct sense of engagement.' Authenticity is central in elite interview panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audacity / willingness to take risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Willingness to take intellectual risks—'courageous risk-takers'—is admired as an indicator of potential high payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists praise those willing to propose projects that could 'reshape or fundamentally challenge' received views. Risk-taking is associated with potential to produce disconfirmable knowledge and significant advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual honesty / integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual honesty and integrity are moral qualities reviewers use to judge applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers look for sincerity, intellectual commitment, and honesty in presentation. Candidates described as having 'intellectual honesty and integrity' and 'non-career-oriented fanatical energy' are favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of the self / control of intellectual trajectory
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of one’s intellectual work and a coherent, self-directed career trajectory are valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists praise applicants who have 'made their own choices' and have reasons for their research directions—signs that distinguish top candidates. This includes a visible career vision and sustained intellectual commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trajectory / demonstrated progress
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate’s trajectory—the pattern of development and demonstrated progress—is considered a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include candidates who overcame weaknesses to reveal talent or who rapidly developed demonstrable expertise; trajectory signals future potential and resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding idiosyncratic taste bias / balancing subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are aware of and sometimes try to counterbalance their own subjective tastes (personal affinities) in evaluating proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter documents idiosyncratic tastes (ex-tennis player preferring body studies, bird enthusiast preferring songbird work) and notes that some panelists (especially in noninterpretative disciplines) actively try to separate taste from competence by focusing on what the project actually tests and its chance of significant results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with disciplinary expectations / methodological fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit between the project’s aims/methods and disciplinary expectations influences evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists’ preferences for more or less theory, or more or less emphasis on social vs intellectual significance, shape assessments. Methodological fit matters: disciplines with heavy technical tools evaluate differently than interpretive fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation in interviews / interpersonal qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: How applicants perform in interviews or discussions (listening, nimbleness, ability to establish exchange) is considered in elite selection contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In settings like the Society of Fellows, interview behavior—establishing exchange, listening, being interesting without dominating—figures into judgments of excellence and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of conflating elegance/cultural capital with merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness that valuing elegance and cultural capital can conflate excellence with elite/upper-middle-class membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that privileging elegance and familiarity with high-status cultural signals may penalize applicants from working-class backgrounds and that these extra-intellectual considerations are not neutral measures of merit.
